```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 150
)
```

This vignette showcases every plotting function in `{stemtools}`: `stem_barplot()`, `stem_inline()`, `stem_battery()`, `stem_multiselect()` and `stem_boxplot()`, and how to save the results as images or native PowerPoint charts. We'll use the simulated `trust` dataset that ships with the package.

```{r setup}
library(stemtools)
library(ggplot2)

data(trust, package = "stemtools")
head(trust)
```

## Setting the Stem theme

`theme_stem()` is a *complete* theme carrying the Stem look. Because it is complete, the plotting functions do not apply it themselves -- instead we switch it on once with `theme_set()` and every plot from here on picks it up automatically:

```{r theme}
theme_set(theme_stem(family = ""))
```

We pass `family = ""` so the plots fall back to the graphics device's default font (the Stem house font, Calibri, may not be installed on every machine). In normal use you would just call `theme_set(theme_stem())`.

The theme is sized for charts exported 19 cm wide: a 13 pt base, 15.6 pt titles and 12 pt data labels. Titles wrap at 73 characters, long category labels on the y axis and in the legend wrap automatically, and the legend uses as many rows as it needs (most 5-point scales fit one). Numbers use the Czech decimal comma.

## How the plotting functions are built

All the plotting functions are composed from a shared frequency core. Each one calls `stem_summarise_cat()` to compute (possibly weighted) proportions with 95% confidence intervals, then hands the aggregated data to a `{ggplot2}` template. You can call the frequency function directly whenever you need the numbers themselves:

```{r summarise}
stem_summarise_cat(trust, item = police, group = eu_index, weight = W)
```

The warning flags cells with fewer than 30 unweighted observations (set `min_cell_n = NULL` to turn it off; the plotting functions never raise it). Other uncertainty measures and the weighted N are available on request:

```{r summarise-variance}
stem_summarise_cat(trust, item = police, weight = W,
                   variance = c("se", "moe", "deff"), n_weighted = TRUE)
```

Variables with `{haven}` value labels (e.g. read from SPSS with `haven::read_sav()`) are converted to factors automatically, so their labels appear in tables and plots.

Every plotting function accepts the same core arguments:

* `item` -- the categorical variable to plot,
* `group` -- an optional grouping variable,
* `weight` -- optional survey weights (passed to `{srvyr}`),
* `palette` and `direction` -- the [Stem colour palette][stem_palette] to use,
* `label_*` -- controls for the percentage labels.

## Simple bar plot

`stem_barplot()` draws the distribution of a single categorical variable as horizontal bars, one bar per category. Single-colour bars use the Stem brand burgundy; `bar_color` changes it.

```{r barplot}
stem_barplot(trust, item = government)
```

Confidence intervals are always computed and can be shown with `errorbar = TRUE`.

```{r barplot-errorbar}
stem_barplot(trust, item = government, errorbar = TRUE)
```

Supplying a `group` variable instead draws one stacked horizontal bar per category of the group, with the item mapped to fill. Proportions are computed *within* each group, so every bar sums to 100%, which makes it easy to compare the composition of the item across groups.

```{r barplot-group}
stem_barplot(trust, item = police, group = eu_index, weight = W)
```

## Inline bar plot

`stem_inline()` is a compact summary of a single variable as one stacked horizontal bar.

```{r inline, fig.height = 2}
stem_inline(trust, item = police, weight = W)
```

## Battery of like items

`stem_battery()` plots several variables that share the same response categories (a Likert battery, say) as one chart, with a stacked bar per item. Pass the items with tidyselect helpers and, optionally, `order_by` to sort the items by their combined share of one or more categories.

```{r battery}
stem_battery(trust,
             items = c(police, eu, government, army, scientists),
             weight = W,
             order_by = c("Definitely Agree", "Rather Agree"))
```

Item labels (the `"label"` attribute) are used automatically when present; set `item_label = FALSE` to use the bare variable names. The items must share the same categories in the same order, and no two items may have the same label; otherwise `stem_battery()` stops with an error saying which items differ.

To give several batteries the same order, pass the order of a "master" battery to `item_order` (as variable names or labels):

```{r battery-order}
stem_battery(trust,
             items = c(police, eu, government, army, scientists),
             item_order = c("scientists", "army"))
```

A long battery can be split into several charts with `items_per_chart`. The items are sorted first, and a list of plots titled "(1/2)", "(2/2)" is returned:

```{r battery-split, fig.height = 3}
parts <- stem_battery(trust,
                      items = c(police, eu, government, army, scientists),
                      order_by = "Definitely Agree",
                      items_per_chart = 3,
                      title = "Trust in institutions")
parts[[1]]
parts[[2]]
```

`collapse_item` collapses the categories of every item at once, as in `stem_barplot()`.

## Multiple-choice items

`stem_multiselect()` summarises a set of "select all that apply" items, rescaling the frequencies so the bars show the share of *respondents* who picked each option (rather than the share of responses).

```{r multiselect}
stem_multiselect(trust, items = dplyr::starts_with("biggest_concern"), weight = W)
```

Supplying a `group` variable draws dodged bars for a within-group comparison, coloured with the nominal palette `"nom"`.

Questions stored as one yes/no column per option (`q5_1` ... `q5_8`, each "Ano"/"Ne") use the yes/no layout: give the answer that marks an option as chosen in `selected`. Each item becomes one bar, named after its label, showing the share of respondents with a valid answer who chose it. `other_levels` keeps options such as "Jiné" at the bottom.

```{r multiselect-yesno}
set.seed(1)
yes_no <- function(p) factor(ifelse(runif(500) < p, "Ano", "Ne"), levels = c("Ano", "Ne"))
media <- data.frame(q5_1 = yes_no(0.7), q5_2 = yes_no(0.45), q5_3 = yes_no(0.3),
                    q5_4 = yes_no(0.6), q5_5 = yes_no(0.1))
attr(media$q5_1, "label") <- "Televize"
attr(media$q5_2, "label") <- "Rozhlas"
attr(media$q5_3, "label") <- "Noviny"
attr(media$q5_4, "label") <- "Internet"
attr(media$q5_5, "label") <- "Jiné"

stem_multiselect(media, items = q5_1:q5_5, selected = "Ano", other_levels = "Jiné")
```

If every option comes out 0 % or every option 100 %, you get a warning: that usually means `selected` doesn't match how the data are coded.

## Customizing labels

By default the plots print a percentage label on each bar (set `labels = FALSE` to hide them). `label_accuracy` controls rounding (`1` for whole numbers, `0.1` for one decimal place), `label_suffix` sets the text appended to each label and `label_hide` suppresses labels for proportions below a threshold (3 % on stacked segments by default; separate bars show every label). On stacked bars each label is white or dark depending on how dark its segment is.

```{r labels}
stem_barplot(trust,
             item = police,
             group = eu_index,
             label_accuracy = 0.1,
             label_hide = 0.1)
```

## Colours

Use `palette` to pick one of the [Stem palettes][stem_palette] and `direction = -1` to reverse it. The diverging palettes also cover 6- and 7-point scales. Colours follow the item's full set of levels, so a scale point nobody chose stays in the legend (as 0 %) and doesn't shift the other colours.

```{r palette}
stem_barplot(trust, item = police, group = eu_index, palette = "div2")
```

For a distribution whose categories have no order (e.g. "What do you heat with?"), use the nominal palette `"nom"`:

```{r palette-nominal}
set.seed(2)
heating <- data.frame(
  source = factor(sample(c("Plyn", "Elektřina", "Dřevo", "Uhlí", "Tepelné čerpadlo"), 600, TRUE,
                         prob = c(0.35, 0.25, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1))),
  region = sample(c("Praha", "Morava", "Čechy"), 600, TRUE)
)
stem_barplot(heating, item = source, group = region, palette = "nom")
```

## Collapsing categories

`collapse_item` and `collapse_group` collapse (or rename) categories by passing a named list, exactly as in `stem_summarise_cat()`.

```{r collapse}
stem_barplot(trust,
             item = police,
             group = eu_index,
             collapse_item = list(`Ano` = c("Definitely Agree", "Rather Agree"),
                                  `Ani ano, ani ne` = "Neither Agree nor Disagree",
                                  `Ne` = c("Rather Disagree", "Definitely Disagree")))
```

## "Don't know" and "other" answers

Name the "don't know" categories in `dk_levels` (in `stem_inline()`, `stem_battery()`, `stem_barplot()` and `stem_multiselect()`). They move to the end, are drawn grey and don't use up a palette colour, so a 5-point scale plus "Nevím" keeps the 5-colour palette. "Other" categories (`other_levels`, in `stem_barplot()` and `stem_multiselect()`) go last too, just before "don't know".

```{r dk, fig.height = 2.5}
trust_dk <- trust
trust_dk$police <- forcats::fct_expand(trust_dk$police, "Nevím")
trust_dk$police[1:80] <- "Nevím"

stem_inline(trust_dk, item = police, dk_levels = "Nevím")
```

```{r dk-bars}
stem_barplot(trust_dk, item = police, dk_levels = "Nevím")
```

## Numeric variables

`stem_boxplot()` draws a numeric variable as horizontal box plots, one per group. Quartiles are weighted: the first value whose cumulative weight share reaches the probability (with equal weights, the same as `quantile(type = 1)`). Whiskers reach the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR, points beyond them are outliers, and the white diamond marks the weighted mean.

```{r boxplot, fig.height = 3}
stem_boxplot(trust, item = age, group = eu_index, weight = W)
```

The same numbers as a table, ready to be combined with other variables (`long = TRUE`):

```{r boxplot-table}
stem_summarise_num(trust, item = age, group = eu_index, weight = W,
                   quantiles = TRUE, return_n = TRUE, n_weighted = TRUE)
```

## Weights

If a `weight` variable is specified, weights are treated as survey weights and passed into `{srvyr}`, which builds a Taylor-series survey design (via the `{survey}` package). `{srvyr}`'s verbs mirror `{dplyr}`, so weighted and unweighted code read the same way.

With unweighted data, the standard errors are computed using the basic $\sqrt{\frac{p \cdot (1-p)}{n}}$ formula. With very small proportions and small samples this can lead to confidence bounds outside of the `(0, 1)` range. With weighted data, the standard errors come from `{srvyr}` using Taylor-series linearization.

```{r weights}
stem_barplot(trust, item = government, weight = W)
```

## Further customization

Every function returns a standard `{ggplot2}` object, so you can keep adding layers, scales and theme tweaks. The global `theme_stem()` is already applied, so this just layers a title on top:

```{r customize}
stem_barplot(trust, item = government) +
  labs(title = "Trust in the government")
```

## Saving charts

`stem_save()` writes a plot as PNG, SVG or PDF, 19 cm wide by default, with a graphics device that renders Calibri. (`ggsave()` picks the ragg device when it is installed, and ragg has been seen to draw Calibri plots as blank images on Windows.) A list of plots, such as a split battery, is saved as numbered files.

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
stem_save(stem_barplot(trust, item = police, group = eu_index), "police.png")
stem_save(parts, "battery.png") # battery_1.png, battery_2.png
```

Bar charts can also go into PowerPoint or Word as *native* charts, whose data can be edited in Excel; box plots, which Office cannot draw, go in as images.

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
stem_export_pptx(
  stem_barplot(trust, item = police, group = eu_index),
  stem_battery(trust, items = c(police, eu, government, army)),
  path = "charts.pptx"
)
```

[stem_palette]: ../reference/stem_palette.html
